Creativity ratings of football actions: JRT results in brief

Summary for discussion: model fit, agreement, rater tendencies

Published

9 November 2026

Data version: 3669 products x 24 raters | 9046 ratings | md5 68037eafc9939992751c2bf646c48a9e. All numbers below are read directly from the analysis output files (results/); nothing was re-estimated for this summary.

At a glance

  • Fit: Raters differ in how they use the 1–7 scale and in how well they separate actions. The most flexible models (GRM, GPCM) fit best by AIC; by BIC the simplest model (M1 (RS-MFRM), rating-scale MFRM) wins narrowly over the GRM.
  • Agreement: Single ratings agree weakly (Krippendorff’s α = .391). The model-based scores have reliability .689 overall. Most actions have only 1–2 ratings, which limits this value.
  • Number of raters: Reliability rises from about .530 with 1 rating to .705 with 2 and passes .80 at 4 ratings per action (model-based simulation). Topping up our actual design to at least 4 ratings per action would give .835.
  • Raters: They differ clearly in strictness, scale use and informativeness, but the final scores barely depend on the model (r = .977 to .996 with the GRM).

Terms used in this summary

Term Plain meaning
IRT / JRT Item response theory treats each rating as a noisy signal of an unobserved quality. Judge response theory (JRT) applies this to raters: rater = “item”, rated action = “person”.
θ (theta) The estimated creativity of an action on a common scale (mean 0, SD 1), adjusted for who rated it.
Threshold (b) How much creativity is needed before a rater moves up to the next scale point. High thresholds = strict rater.
Discrimination (a) How sharply a rater’s ratings separate less from more creative actions. Higher = more consistent with the shared scale.
Information How much one rating by a given rater reduces uncertainty about θ. Depends on a and on where the thresholds sit.
Reliability Share of score variance that is true differences rather than noise (0–1).
rel_post Reliability of one action’s score, from its posterior uncertainty (1 − PSD²).
AIC / BIC Fit indices that penalise complexity; lower is better. BIC penalises extra parameters more strongly.

Why a model at all? The design is sparse: each action was rated by only a few of the 24 raters (mean 2.47, median 2 ratings per action; 10% of the action × rater matrix is filled). A plain average then depends on which raters an action happened to get. JRT puts all ratings on one scale while accounting for rater differences.

Design snapshot

1. Model fit: which assumptions hold?

We fitted four models that make increasingly fewer assumptions about the raters.

Reading: Both likelihood-ratio tests and AIC favour giving each rater their own thresholds and their own discrimination. BIC, which penalises the extra parameters strongly, prefers the simplest model by a small margin (ΔBIC for the GRM = 4.2). In the GPCM, the most discriminating rater’s value is 7.3 times that of the least discriminating one. Figure 2 shows the same spread in the GRM.

Does the model choice change the scores?

Barely. The table compares each model’s action scores with the GRM scores.

Raw mean ratings versus GRM scores: Kendall’s τb = .833 (1 rating), .818 (2 ratings), .849 (3+ ratings). Actions with the same raw mean can differ by up to 2.17 SD on θ, because the model accounts for who rated them.

Checks. The GRM converged (436 iterations). A global fit statistic (C2) cannot be computed because 30 of 276 rater pairs share no action. Re-fitting with the 4 excluded low-volume raters changes almost nothing (θ correlation 0.9999; reliability .688 vs .689).

2. Agreement and reliability

Different indices answer different questions, which is why their values differ so much.

Reading: Raters agree only modestly on individual ratings (α = .391). Combining several ratings in the model gives usable scores (.689). If every action had at least 4 ratings, reliability would rise to .835 (simulation). This keeps the actual raters and adds 6,778 ratings by randomly drawn raters to the 3,007 actions with fewer than 4. The same simulation run on the actual design gives .686, close to the observed .689. A full panel (all 24 raters rate every action) would reach .969, but that design is far from ours.

3. Rater tendencies

Leniency and strictness

Strictness spans 2.25 logits from the most lenient (R24, mean rating 3.75) to the strictest rater (R06, mean 1.76). M1 summarises strictness in one number per rater. The GRM thresholds show the same pattern in more detail.

Use of the scale

8 of 24 raters never used at least one scale point; in every case this included the top category (7). Floor use varies widely: R06 gave a “1” in 58% of ratings, others rarely did.

Informativeness

Information per rating ranges from 0.13 (R18) to 2.52 (R26). Information adds up across ratings, so one rating by the top rater carries as much as several ratings by the least informative one. Raters with few ratings have wide intervals, so their rank is uncertain.

Rater overview

Info share = this rater’s share of the total information of the full panel. Infit/outfit values below 1 mostly reflect the design (about two ratings per action), not misfit.

4. Research questions in one line

Descriptive summary for discussion; interpretation is still open.

  • RQ1. Reliability and number of ratings. The actual scores reach .689 (single ratings: α = .391); with at least 4 ratings per action they would reach .835 (simulation). Reliability per action rises from .522 with 1 rating to .699 with 2 and passes .80 from about 4 ratings.
  • RQ2. Rater differences. Raters differ in strictness (range 2.25 logits), scale use (8 leave points unused), discrimination (7.3-fold) and information. The estimates are precise for high-volume raters and uncertain for low-volume ones.
  • RQ3a. Are the simpler models’ constraints tenable? Not by LR tests and AIC: rater-specific thresholds (χ²(105) = 840.45) and discriminations (χ²(23) = 156.59) both improve fit, p < .001. BIC narrowly prefers the simplest model.
  • RQ3b. Do scores change? Little. Correlations with the GRM are .977–.996, but 15%–21% of actions change quintile under the Rasch-family models. Raw means and GRM scores rank actions with τb = .818–.849.
